title: Export SRT Subtitles on iPhone for an Editable Caption Track
description: Export SRT when you need subtitles as an editable timed-text file separate from the video.
direct: Export an SRT when the recipient wants separate, editable subtitles. Pair it with the exact video cut you used to check the timing.

cards.choice.heading: SRT is a sidecar
cards.choice.body: An SRT contains caption text and start/end times. It does not contain your video. YouTube supports basic UTF-8 SRT but does not recognize styling markup, so do not expect animated word highlights to transfer.
sections.explain.heading: Check synchronization after editing
sections.explain.body: A subtitle file can be correct for one cut and wrong for another. Removing an introduction, changing playback speed or moving a scene can shift later captions. Keep a clear shared filename for the video and subtitle version. Check several points through a long clip rather than only the first line.
sections.practice.heading: Choose the right export
sections.practice.body: Our app offers SRT text and captioned MP4/MOV exports. Core caption generation can run on device; optional online AI text tools require consent. A separate SRT lets the destination render captions, while a captioned video carries their visible appearance. Free single-video exports include a Just Captions watermark; Pro unlocks further features. This is caption creation from speech, not removal or extraction of already burned-in text.
faqs.reader-question-1.heading: Will my animated word highlights appear from the SRT on YouTube?
faqs.reader-question-1.body: Do not rely on SRT for your animated style. Export a captioned video when the visual treatment needs to travel with the picture.
faqs.reader-question-2.heading: The first caption lines up but the last one does not. What now?
faqs.reader-question-2.body: Check for a cut or speed change after captioning. Use the final video, then check the beginning, middle and end before sending it with the SRT.
